title: The 3 AM Outage
subtitle: Checkout went dark for 27 minutes on a Friday night. The rollback fixed it, but nobody knows why it broke.

inspiredBy.title: Cloudflare global outage
inspiredBy.summary: On 2 July 2019, Cloudflare pushed a new WAF rule containing a regular expression vulnerable to catastrophic backtracking. Deployed globally at once, it pinned CPUs on every edge server and caused widespread 502 errors for about 27 minutes, until the WAF was disabled with a global kill switch.

briefing:
**Monday, 09:12. Shipfast HQ.**

Friday, a little after 3 AM local time, checkout died. For about **27 minutes** customers could browse but not pay. Someone rolled checkout back and everything recovered. Nobody knows *why* it broke.

The RCA is on your desk, due today: a timeline, a root cause and who was affected.

The **evidence pack** holds what on-call collected: nginx and app logs, metrics, the Postgres slow log, deploys, the Slack channel and the service's git history. **Read `README_FIRST.txt` first**, and watch the time zones: not every source agrees on what time it is.

Six stages follow a real RCA: **when** it started, **what changed**, **what triggered** it, **where in the code**, **why it kept going**, and the **blast radius**. Each answer is a small, exact value. Stuck? Use the Toolbox and the hints.
setupChecklist: Get the evidence: download and unzip the **evidence pack**, *or* open the **Evidence Explorer** to browse every file in your browser (no installs).
Note each source's time zone: nginx, Postgres and deploys are **UTC**, the app log is **local time (+02:00)**, metrics and Slack use **epoch seconds**.
Pick your path: **bash** (Linux, macOS or WSL), **Windows PowerShell** (every Toolbox command has a PowerShell version), or the **browser Explorer**.
Git is optional: `repo/git-log.txt` holds the full history (with diffs) as plain text.

evidence.description: Briefing notes from the on-call team, the file list and important notes on time formats. Start here.
Every HTTP request through the edge proxy during the night, with status, timings, request id (`rid`) and customer id (`cid`).
The `log_format` definition and proxy timeouts, so you can tell what each field (and each timestamp) means.
Structured logs from the checkout service pods: request lifecycle, versions, warnings, restarts. Check the timestamp offset.
Checkout service metrics at 15-second resolution: pods ready, CPU, event-loop lag, p99 latency, RPS, error rate, restarts.
Slow-query log and notable events from the primary database.
Deploys and rollbacks across all services for the last few days.
The incident channel, as exported. `ts` is epoch seconds stored as a string. Treat opinions in it as hypotheses, not facts.
The full history of the checkout service repo, tags included. Clone it with `git clone shipfast-checkout.bundle`.
The same repo history as plain text: every commit, tag and diff (`git log -p --decorate --all`). Use it if you don't have git.

rules: Work only from the evidence pack. Don't read the generator source or the site's source code; that spoils the fun.
Answers are case-insensitive, and leading and trailing whitespace is ignored. Stick to the format shown under each question.
Each hint costs the points shown on it. Hints are revealed in order, from a gentle nudge to almost the full command.
Working in pairs is encouraged. Talk through your reasoning out loud, just like a real incident review.
Any tool is allowed: grep, awk, jq, Python, a spreadsheet, your favourite editor. The Toolbox tab lists commands that help.
Wrong answers cost nothing, so guess freely. Still, try to be able to explain *why* your answer is right.
Don't share flags with other teams until everyone is done. Sharing techniques is fine.
Careful with the code you find: some of it is slow on purpose. Read the Toolbox warning before you run any regex experiments.

stage.name: When did it start?
stage.goal: Find the exact UTC time of the first server error users saw.
lookFor: `nginx/access.log` is in UTC and logs when a request *ended*
The status is the 3-digit number right after the quoted request
Any 5xx counts, on any path
Take the earliest timestamp, not just the first line you see
stage.explorerTip: Open `nginx/access.log` and add a **regex** filter `" 5\d\d ` to keep only 5xx lines. Use **First match** to jump to the earliest hit and check the **histogram by minute** to see where errors cluster. The time inside `[...]` is already UTC.

questions.title: When did it start?
questions.prompt:
When did users first see errors?

Find the **first** request in `nginx/access.log` that returned a server error (**any status 500–599**, any path).

Answer with its time **in UTC** as `HH:MM:SS` (no date, no milliseconds).

hints.text: The status code is a field of its own on every nginx line. Look at `nginx/nginx.conf.snippet` to see which position it sits in. The log is already in chronological order, so the first match is your answer.
Split each line on spaces. The status lands in field `$9` (count it against the `log_format`). Filter for statuses that start with `5`, then stop at the first hit.

Something like:

```sh
awk '$9 ~ /^5[0-9][0-9]$/ {print $4, $9, $7; exit}' nginx/access.log
```

Then strip the date part from the `[dd/Mon/yyyy:HH:MM:SS` field. Don't convert the time: nginx already logs UTC here.

questions.successNote: nginx's `$time_local` records when the request **finished**, not when it started. A request that hung for 30 seconds is logged 30 seconds after the damage began. Always ask *what moment a timestamp represents* and *which time zone it's in* before you line up sources.

stage.name: What changed?
stage.goal: Identify the commit checkout was actually running when the errors began.
lookFor: `deploys/deploys.log` lists each release with its short commit
Several services deployed that night; only one serves checkout
Compare deploy times with your stage 1 answer
Slack opinions are not evidence
stage.explorerTip: Open `deploys/deploys.log` and filter **contains** `service=checkout`. Find the last checkout deploy *before* your first 5xx (both are UTC). Then open `repo/git-log.txt`, filter **contains** that version tag and use **First match** to confirm the commit.

questions.title: What changed?
questions.prompt:
Which **commit was checkout actually running when the errors started**? Find the deployed release, then its commit in the repo.

Answer with the **7-character short SHA** (lowercase hex).

hints.text: Put your Q1 timestamp next to `deploys/deploys.log`. Which checkout deploy was *live* at that moment? The most recent one, or one before it? The app log's `version` field per line confirms what each pod was really running.

Clone the bundle and match the deployed **version** to a **git tag**. `git show <tag>` tells you which commit a tag points to. The deploy log's `commit=` field should agree with it. If two candidates remain, read both diffs and ask which one could plausibly freeze a pod.

```sh
git clone repo/shipfast-checkout.bundle && cd shipfast-checkout
git tag --sort=creatordate | tail -5
git log --oneline -1 <tag>      # short SHA of the tagged commit
git show <tag> --stat           # what did that release touch?
```

Cross-check: `grep checkout deploys/deploys.log` and the `version` field in the app log right before the first error.

questions.successNote: The most recent deploy is the first suspect, not automatically the culprit. One release went out over half an hour before anything broke, so recency alone would have sent you the wrong way. Correlate *when each change went live* with *when symptoms began*, and then confirm it by reading the diff.

stage.name: What triggered it?
stage.goal: Find the order whose checkout started but never finished.
lookFor: `app/checkout-service.log` is JSON lines in *local* time (+02:00)
Each checkout logs a start and, normally, a done
Look just before the first errors, after converting time zones
A frozen pod goes silent, then lags, then restarts
stage.explorerTip: Use the **time converter** widget to turn your stage 1 UTC time into +02:00. Open `app/checkout-service.log`, add the **JSON field filter** `msg = checkout.start` and look at starts shortly before that time. Filter **contains** each candidate order ID: the one with no `checkout.done` is your suspect.

questions.title: What triggered it?
questions.prompt:
One order in the checkout service log **started but never finished**: a `checkout.start` with no matching `checkout.done`, after which the pod went quiet.

Which **order ID** is that "poison" order?

hints.text: `app/checkout-service.log` is JSON lines in **local time (+02:00)**, while nginx is UTC. Convert your Q1 time before you go looking. Remember nginx logged the *end* of a request that timed out after 30 seconds.

Look at `checkout.start` lines from about 30 seconds before the first 5xx. For each order, check whether a `checkout.done` with the same `order` ever appears. You can also follow the `rid` of the first failing nginx request into the app log.

```sh
# starts vs dones per order, then diff them
jq -r 'select(.msg=="checkout.start") | .order' app/checkout-service.log | sort -u > started
jq -r 'select(.msg=="checkout.done")  | .order' app/checkout-service.log | sort -u > done
comm -23 started done
# or: grep '<rid-from-nginx>' app/checkout-service.log
```

questions.successNote: Some bugs only fire on specific input. A deploy can look healthy for 15 minutes until the one payload that triggers it arrives. A request that **starts and never ends** (no completion log, no error) is a classic sign that a thread or event loop is stuck rather than crashing.

stage.name: Where in the code?
stage.goal: Find the function in the bad release that can block Node's event loop.
lookFor: Look at what the bad release changed, not the whole repo
Nested quantifiers like `(x+)*` can backtrack catastrophically
The poison order's log line hints at what kind of input it carried
The answer is a function name, not a file name
stage.explorerTip: Open `repo/git-log.txt` (the full `git log -p`). Filter **contains** the release tag from stage 2 and use **First match** to jump to that commit, then filter **regex** `^\+.*(function|RegExp|=\s*/\^)` to see only the added lines that define functions or regexes.

questions.title: Where in the code?
questions.prompt:
Something in that release takes a very long time on certain input and blocks the whole Node.js process.

Which **function** contains the dangerous code? Answer with its name **exactly as in the source** (no parentheses, no path).

hints.text: Look at what the poison order had that most orders didn't. The app log has some extra fields on `checkout.start`. Then read the diff of the release you found in Q2.
The release added new input handling. Look for a **regular expression** in the diff, specifically one with a quantifier *inside* a group that is itself quantified, like `( ... + ... )*`.

```sh
git show <bad-sha> --stat
git show <bad-sha> -- src/
git grep -n -E 'RegExp|/\^.*\)\*' <bad-sha>
```

The answer is the exported function that *uses* the suspicious regex, not the constant's name.

questions.successNote: **Catastrophic backtracking:** with nested quantifiers like `(\w+\s?)*`, a backtracking regex engine can split a string of words in exponentially many ways. When the final character makes the match fail, it tries **all** of them. 99 characters is enough to keep a CPU busy for far longer than anyone will wait, and in single-threaded Node.js that blocks everything.

stage.name: Why did it keep going?
stage.goal: Count how many times the poison order was submitted in total.
lookFor: Every submission logs its own start line with a new request id
Retries and repeat clicks land on different pods
Count submissions, not every log line that mentions the order
Include the first one
stage.explorerTip: In `app/checkout-service.log`, add the **JSON field filter** `order = <your stage 3 order>` plus `msg = checkout.start`; the match count is your answer. Cross-check with **Count unique** using the regex `"rid":"([0-9a-f]+)"`.

questions.title: Why did it keep going?
questions.prompt:
One bad request freezes one pod, yet the outage lasted ~27 minutes. Something kept **re-poisoning** the service.

How many times **in total** was the poison order submitted to checkout? Answer with an **integer, including the first**.

hints.text: Every submission of an order produces a fresh request, with a new `rid`, but the order ID stays the same. Count how often that order *started*.

Count `checkout.start` lines for the poison order in the app log. Cross-check against nginx: the same customer's `POST /api/checkout` requests that ended in 5xx. Watch which pod each attempt landed on, and what happened to that pod next.

```sh
jq -c 'select(.msg=="checkout.start" and .order=="ORD-XXXXXX") | {ts, pod, rid}' \
  app/checkout-service.log | wc -l
```

questions.successNote: Client **retries** (automatic, plus impatient users clicking again) kept sending the same poison payload. Round-robin load balancing spread it across every pod, and **liveness probes** restarted frozen pods straight back into the line of fire. Retries need backoff and caps, and the system needs a way to reject inputs that killed it before. Otherwise self-healing just becomes self-reinfecting.

stage.name: Blast radius
stage.goal: Count the distinct real customers who got a 5xx on checkout.
lookFor: Only `POST /api/checkout` lines with a 500–599 status
Use the whole file, not just the incident window
The customer is the `cid=` field at the end of each line
Drop `cid=-` and `cid=cus_synthetic`
stage.explorerTip: Open `nginx/access.log`, add a **regex** filter `"POST /api/checkout [^"]*" 5\d\d `, add **NOT** filters for `cid=-` and `cid=cus_synthetic`, then run **Count unique** with the regex `cid=(\S+)`. The number of unique values is your answer.

questions.title: Blast radius
questions.prompt:
How many **real customers** were hit?

Count the **distinct `cid=` values** with **at least one 5xx** (500–599) on **`POST /api/checkout`**, anywhere in `nginx/access.log` (whole file).

Exclude `cid=-` (anonymous) and `cid=cus_synthetic` (our monitor). Answer with an **integer**.

hints.text: You need three filters (method + path, status class, real customer), then a *distinct* count. Don't count requests: one customer retrying five times is still one customer.
Match lines with `"POST /api/checkout ` and a status of `5xx` in field `$9`. Extract the `cid=` value (the last field), drop `-` and `cus_synthetic`, then `sort -u | wc -l`.

```sh
awk '$6=="\"POST" && $7=="/api/checkout" && $9 ~ /^5/ {print $NF}' nginx/access.log \
  | sed 's/^cid=//' | grep -v -x -e '-' -e 'cus_synthetic' \
  | sort -u | wc -l
```

questions.successNote: Blast radius decides the response: who gets an apology email, whether the status page says "some" or "most" users, and whether failed payments need reconciling. Count **people**, not requests, and remember to filter out your own synthetic traffic, which would otherwise inflate the impact.

items.title: Unpack the evidence
items.explain: Extracts the pack. Everything lives under one top-level folder.

items.title: See what you've got
items.explain: Lists every file recursively with sizes. A huge file is usually the one worth sampling first.

items.title: Peek at the first lines
items.explain: Look at the format **before** you parse it. `tail -n 5` shows the end of the window.

items.title: How big is it?
items.explain: Line counts tell you whether you can eyeball a file or need to aggregate it.

items.title: Browse without wrapping
items.explain: `-S` chops long lines instead of wrapping them. Use `/pattern` to search, `n` for the next hit, `G` for the end of the file.

items.title: What kind of file is this?
items.explain: Identifies file types: text, JSON, git bundle, and so on.
items.powershell:
Get-ChildItem repo, metrics | Select-Object Name, Length
Get-Content metrics\checkout_metrics.csv -TotalCount 2

items.title: Read the README
items.explain: Seriously. It has notes on formats and time zones.

items.title: Count matches
items.explain: `-c` prints the number of matching lines instead of the lines themselves. Fast sanity checks.

items.title: Extended regex
items.explain: `-E` enables alternation `|`, `+`, `{n}` and so on without backslashes. The leading `" ` anchors the match right after the request string.

items.title: Line numbers
items.explain: `-n` prefixes each hit with its line number, which helps you jump there in `less` (`<num>G`).

items.title: Stop at the first match
items.explain: `-m1` exits after the first hit. On a chronologically sorted log, that gives you the *earliest* occurrence.

items.title: Invert / exclude
items.explain: `-v` keeps lines that do **not** match. Each `-e` adds another pattern. Great for removing health checks and synthetic noise.

items.title: Print only the match
items.command: grep -o 'cid=[^ ]*' nginx/access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
items.explain: `-o` outputs just the matched text, which makes it ideal for extracting one field from messy lines.
items.powershell: Select-String -Path nginx\access.log -Pattern 'cid=\S+' | ForEach-Object { $_.Matches[0].Value } | Group-Object | Sort-Object Count -Descending | Select-Object -First 10 Count, Name

items.title: Context around a hit
items.explain: `-B`/`-A` show lines before and after each match, so you see what happened around an event.

items.title: Search compressed logs
items.explain: In real life old logs are gzipped. `zgrep`/`zcat` read them without unpacking.

items.title: Pull fields from nginx lines
items.explain: awk splits on whitespace. In this format: `$1` IP, `$4` `[time`, `$6` `"METHOD`, `$7` path, `$9` status, `$NF` `cid=...`. Verify against the `log_format`.

items.title: Status code histogram
items.explain: The classic first look at any access log: how many of each status code.
items.powershell: Select-String -Path nginx\access.log -Pattern '" (\d{3}) ' | ForEach-Object { $_.Matches[0].Groups[1].Value } | Group-Object | Sort-Object Count -Descending | Select-Object Count, Name

items.title: Filter by field
items.explain: awk conditions on fields are more precise than grep, because a `500` can also show up in a byte count.

items.title: Bucket per minute
items.explain: `substr($4,14,5)` pulls out `HH:MM` from `[13/Nov/2026:HH:MM:SS`. Since the log is sorted, `uniq -c` gives a per-minute count. Use `,8)` for per-second.
items.powershell: Select-String -Path nginx\access.log -Pattern ':(\d\d:\d\d):\d\d \+0000\] "[^"]*" 5\d\d ' | ForEach-Object { $_.Matches[0].Groups[1].Value } | Group-Object | Select-Object Count, Name

items.title: Per-minute with cut
items.explain: `cut` on `:` gives `HH:MM` from the timestamp. Cruder than awk, but quick.
items.powershell: Select-String -Path nginx\access.log -Pattern ':(\d\d:\d\d):\d\d ' | ForEach-Object { $_.Matches[0].Groups[1].Value } | Group-Object | Select-Object -First 10 Count, Name

items.title: Group by two fields
items.command: awk '{print $7, $9}' nginx/access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -20
items.explain: Which path + status combinations dominate? Great for seeing *which* endpoints fail.
items.powershell: Select-String -Path nginx\access.log -Pattern '"\w+ (\S+) [^"]*" (\d{3}) ' | ForEach-Object { $_.Matches[0].Groups[1].Value + ' ' + $_.Matches[0].Groups[2].Value } | Group-Object | Sort-Object Count -Descending | Select-Object -First 20 Count, Name

items.title: Count unique values
items.explain: `sort -u` removes duplicates, and `wc -l` counts what's left. Distinct users, IPs, rids, and so on.

items.title: First and last occurrence
items.explain: Prints the first and last matching lines, which gives you the start and end of a phenomenon in one go.

items.title: Pretty-print one line
items.explain: See every field a log line carries before you write filters.

items.title: Filter by message
items.explain: `select()` keeps matching objects, and `-c` keeps them one per line so you can still grep, head and wc.
items.powershell: Select-String -Path app\checkout-service.log -Pattern '"msg":"checkout.start"' | ForEach-Object { $_.Line | ConvertFrom-Json } | Select-Object -First 10 ts, pod, order, customer

items.title: Follow one order
items.explain: Every event for a single order. Is there a start *and* a done?
items.powershell: Select-String -Path app\checkout-service.log -Pattern 'ORD-XXXXXX' -SimpleMatch | ForEach-Object { $_.Line | ConvertFrom-Json } | Format-Table ts, pod, msg, order, rid

items.title: Custom output with -r
items.explain: `-r` prints raw strings, and `\(...)` interpolates fields. `//` gives a default when a field is missing.

items.title: What message types exist?
items.explain: A histogram of event types. Rare warnings stand out immediately.
items.powershell: Select-String -Path app\checkout-service.log -Pattern '"msg":"([^"]+)"' | ForEach-Object { $_.Matches[0].Groups[1].Value } | Group-Object | Sort-Object Count -Descending | Select-Object Count, Name

items.title: Group and count (slurp)
items.command: jq -s 'map(select(.level=="warn")) | group_by(.msg) | map({msg: .[0].msg, n: length})' app/checkout-service.log
items.explain: `-s` slurps all lines into one array, so you can `group_by`, `sort_by` and `length` across the whole file.
items.powershell: Select-String -Path app\checkout-service.log -Pattern '"level":"warn"' | ForEach-Object { $_.Line | ConvertFrom-Json } | Group-Object msg | Select-Object Count, Name

items.title: Filter on numbers
items.explain: Numeric comparisons and object construction `{a, b}` keep only the fields you care about.
items.powershell: Select-String -Path app\checkout-service.log -Pattern 'eventloop.lag' -SimpleMatch | ForEach-Object { $_.Line | ConvertFrom-Json } | Where-Object { $_.lag_ms -gt 1000 } | Format-Table ts, pod, lag_ms

items.title: Versions over time
items.explain: `@tsv` turns arrays into tab-separated lines. Combined with `uniq`, you see when each pod switched version.

items.title: Grab a request id from nginx
items.explain: nginx and the checkout service share the `rid` (request id), which is the thread you pull to link both sides of a request.

items.title: Find that request in the app log
items.explain: The same request from the service's point of view: which pod, which order, which version, and did it finish?

items.title: All requests for one customer
items.explain: Retries from the same person line up here. Watch the timing between attempts.

items.title: Line up two sources by time
items.explain: Merge events from different files into one view, **but only after they're all in the same time zone**.
items.powershell: Select-String -Path deploys\deploys.log, db\postgresql-slow.log -Pattern '01:2\d' | ForEach-Object Line | Sort-Object | Select-Object -First 20

items.title: Requests that never finished
items.explain: `comm -23` prints lines only in the first sorted list: things that started but have no matching end.

items.title: Pod timeline
items.explain: One pod's life story. Gaps (silence) can be as telling as errors.

items.title: Epoch to UTC
items.explain: Converts unix epoch seconds to a human UTC time (GNU date). On macOS: `date -u -r 1794531600`.

items.title: UTC to local (Israel)
items.explain: Shows what a UTC instant was on the office clock. In November, Israel is **UTC+02:00**.

items.title: Local to UTC
items.explain: Normalizes an offset timestamp (like the app log's) to UTC. `+%H:%M:%S` sets the output format.

items.title: Python one-liner
items.command: python3 -c 'from datetime import datetime, timezone; print(datetime.fromtimestamp(1794531600, timezone.utc))'
items.explain: Same conversion, but portable. Swap in `timezone(timedelta(hours=2))` to get local time.
items.powershell:
# no Python needed on Windows:
[DateTimeOffset]::FromUnixTimeSeconds(1794531600).ToString('yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss zzz')

items.title: Human time to epoch
items.explain: Handy for finding the matching row in an epoch-indexed file like the metrics CSV.

items.title: Convert a whole CSV column
items.command: awk -F, 'NR>1 {cmd="date -u -d @"$1" +%H:%M:%S"; cmd | getline t; close(cmd); print t, $0}' metrics/checkout_metrics.csv | head
items.explain: Prefix every metrics row with a readable UTC time. Slow-ish (it forks `date` per row), but fine for a few hundred rows.

items.title: Slack timestamps
items.explain: Slack `ts` is an epoch *string* with a fractional part. `tonumber | floor | todate` gives ISO-8601 UTC.

items.title: Pretty table
items.explain: Aligns CSV columns so you can actually read them. `-s,` sets the separator and `-t` builds a table.

items.title: Show the header with column numbers
items.explain: Numbers each column, so you know which `$N` to use in awk.

items.title: Select columns
items.explain: `-F,` splits on commas. Print just the columns you're investigating.
items.powershell: Import-Csv metrics\checkout_metrics.csv | Select-Object -First 10 ts_epoch, cpu_pct_max, eventloop_lag_p99_ms

items.title: First row over a threshold
items.explain: Finds when a metric first crosses a line (here, the error-rate column). Then convert `$1` with `date -u -d @...`.

items.title: All rows over a threshold
items.explain: Shows the full span of an anomaly: when it started, when it ended, and whether it was continuous.
items.powershell: Import-Csv metrics\checkout_metrics.csv | Where-Object { [double]$_.eventloop_lag_p99_ms -gt 1000 } | Select-Object ts_epoch, eventloop_lag_p99_ms

items.title: Min / max of a column
items.command: awk -F, 'NR>1 {if($2<m||m=="")m=$2; if($2>M)M=$2} END{print m, M}' metrics/checkout_metrics.csv
items.explain: Quick range check: did pods_ready ever hit zero?

items.title: Clone a bundle
items.explain: A bundle is a whole repo in one file. Cloning it gives you a normal working copy with full history and tags. No git? `repo/git-log.txt` holds the same history as plain text (`git log -p --decorate --all`).
items.powershell:
# git is optional: read repo\git-log.txt instead
Get-Content repo\git-log.txt | Out-Host -Paging

items.title: History at a glance
items.explain: `--decorate` shows tags and branches next to commits, so you can see where each release sits. No git? `repo/git-log.txt` holds the same history as plain text (`git log -p --decorate --all`).
items.powershell:
# git is optional: read repo\git-log.txt instead
Select-String -Path repo\git-log.txt -Pattern '^commit ' -Context 0,5 | Select-Object -First 30

items.title: List tags
items.explain: Releases in order. Match them against the versions in deploy logs. No git? `repo/git-log.txt` holds the same history as plain text (`git log -p --decorate --all`).
items.powershell:
# git is optional: read repo\git-log.txt instead
Select-String -Path repo\git-log.txt -Pattern 'tag: [^,)]+' -AllMatches | ForEach-Object { $_.Matches.Value }

items.title: What's in a release?
items.explain: Commit message, author, date and the files touched by the commit a tag points to. No git? `repo/git-log.txt` holds the same history as plain text (`git log -p --decorate --all`).
items.powershell:
# git is optional: read repo\git-log.txt instead
Select-String -Path repo\git-log.txt -Pattern 'tag: v2.14.1\b' -Context 0,60

items.title: Diff two releases
items.explain: Everything that changed between two versions. Drop `--stat` for the full patch. No git? `repo/git-log.txt` holds the same history as plain text (`git log -p --decorate --all`).
items.powershell:
# git is optional: read repo\git-log.txt instead
Select-String -Path repo\git-log.txt -Pattern '^commit |^\+\+\+ b/' | Select-Object -First 40 Line

items.title: Find who added a string
items.explain: The "pickaxe": commits that added or removed occurrences of `pattern`, with their patches. No git? `repo/git-log.txt` holds the same history as plain text (`git log -p --decorate --all`).
items.powershell:
# git is optional: read repo\git-log.txt instead
Select-String -Path repo\git-log.txt -Pattern '^commit |^[+-].*pattern' | ForEach-Object Line

items.title: Search code at a revision
items.explain: Greps the tree as it was at that tag, without checking it out. No git? `repo/git-log.txt` holds the same history as plain text (`git log -p --decorate --all`).
items.powershell:
# git is optional: read repo\git-log.txt instead
Select-String -Path repo\git-log.txt -Pattern 'pattern' -Context 2,2

items.title: Blame a line range
items.explain: Who last touched each line, and in which commit. Add `-w` to ignore whitespace changes. No git? `repo/git-log.txt` holds the same history as plain text (`git log -p --decorate --all`).
items.powershell:
# git is optional: read repo\git-log.txt instead
Select-String -Path repo\git-log.txt -Pattern '^commit |^Author:|^\+\+\+ b/src/path/to/file.ts' | ForEach-Object Line

items.title: Time a regex in Node (SAFE sizes only)
items.command: node -e 'const re=/^(a+)+$/; for (let n=18;n<=26;n++){const s="a".repeat(n)+"!"; const t=Date.now(); re.test(s); console.log(n, Date.now()-t, "ms")}'
items.explain:
Measures how long a regex takes to **fail** on inputs of growing length that end in a char it can't match. `(a+)+` is the textbook evil pattern; swap in any regex you're suspicious of (and an input shape that suits it). If the time roughly **doubles per extra character**, it's exponential.

**WARNING: never go above ~28 characters.** Each extra char doubles the runtime, so a few more and your terminal is frozen for minutes, or years. If that happens, `Ctrl+C`, or `pkill node` from another terminal.

items.title: Same test in Python
items.command:
python3 -c '
import re, time
for n in range(18, 25):
    s = "a" * n + "!"
    t = time.time()
    re.match(r"^(a+)+$", s)
    print(n, round((time.time() - t) * 1000), "ms")
'
items.explain: Python's `re` is also a backtracking engine and blows up the same way. Paste it as-is: the multi-line string inside single quotes is fine in bash and zsh. **Same warning: keep n small.**

items.title: Run with a hard timeout
items.explain: A safety net: kills the process after 10 seconds no matter what.
items.powershell:
$re = New-Object Text.RegularExpressions.Regex('^(a+)+$', 'None', [TimeSpan]::FromSeconds(5))
try { $re.IsMatch(('a' * 40) + '!') } catch { 'timed out after 5s' }

items.title: Compare to a linear version
items.command: node -e 'const re=/^[\w\s]*$/; const s="a ".repeat(5000)+"!"; console.time("t"); re.test(s); console.timeEnd("t")'
items.explain: A character class with a single quantifier can't backtrack exponentially. Even on 10,000 characters it finishes in well under a millisecond.

items.title: All slow statements
items.explain: Every line that logged a query duration.

items.title: Queries slower than X ms
items.explain: Finds the `duration:` token and prints the timestamp and duration when it's above 2000 ms. Adjust the threshold to taste.

items.title: Slow queries per minute
items.explain: Characters 12–16 are `HH:MM` in `2026-11-13 HH:MM:SS UTC`. A histogram shows *when* the DB was struggling, and also when it went *quiet*.
items.powershell: Select-String -Path db\postgresql-slow.log -Pattern '^\S+ (\d\d:\d\d).*duration:' | ForEach-Object { $_.Matches[0].Groups[1].Value } | Group-Object | Select-Object Count, Name

items.title: Who connected?
items.explain: Shows sessions opening, and which application opened them (backup jobs, migrations, apps).

items.title: Non-query events
items.explain: Checkpoints, connections, COPY: the background activity around the queries.
